findings.title: The operator console is registered outside the Fastify scope that carries the session hook, so every /admin route is unauthenticated
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: admin routes outside the auth scope
findings.evidence: server.js:27-34 registers authPlugin and rateLimitPlugin inside an anonymous plugin function (apiScope) mounted at prefix /api/v1. plugins/auth.js:40 adds its onRequest hook with fastify.addHook inside that plugin, and plugins/auth.js is a plain async function — grep confirms fastify-plugin is not a dependency and fp() is not called anywhere in the tree, so the plugin is encapsulated and its hook applies only to apiScope and its children. server.js:38 registers adminRoutes as a sibling at prefix /admin, outside that encapsulation. The author believed otherwise: routes/admin.js:6-8 states 'The session hook populates request.user with the operator's identity before any of these handlers run', and routes/admin.js:15 defensively falls back to 'system' when request.user is absent — which is what it will always be, because fastify.decorateRequest('user', null) at plugins/auth.js:38 is scoped the same way. The requireRole decorator at plugins/auth.js:58 has zero call sites in the tree. path_coverage.py independently flagged '/admin' [server.js:38] and '/config' [routes/admin.js:22] as unguarded siblings of a guarded '/internal'.
findings.impact: Anonymous callers reach the whole operator surface: DELETE /admin/tenants/:id destroys every notification row and the tenant record (lib/store.js:94-97) with no credential at all; GET /admin/tenants/:id/notifications reads any tenant's messages; GET /admin/config returns internal configuration; POST /admin/sessions/impersonate is exposed. The same gap removes the rate limiter from /admin, /hooks and /healthz.
findings.recommendation: Register adminRoutes inside a scope that installs the auth hook, or wrap plugins/auth.js in fastify-plugin and add the hook at the root, then gate each admin handler on fastify.requireRole(request, 'operator'). Add a route-level test that asserts 401 for every /admin verb with no Authorization header.

triage.reason: There is no unskippable layer. The only auth hook in the tree is plugins/auth.js:40 and its encapsulation boundary is server.js:27-34; no proxy, gateway or second hook covering /admin exists in this tree.
server.js:59 binds 0.0.0.0 and the routes act on tenant data belonging to other principals, so a second principal is crossed.

The comment at server.js:36-37 says the console is served from its own hostname, but nothing in the tree enforces host separation — no host constraint on the route, no proxy config in the repo. Under FP-08 an unevidenced external control is UNKNOWN, and here even that is absent.

findings.title: Saved-filter search builds its WHERE clause from attacker-chosen column names
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: SQL injection via filter column names in searchNotifications
findings.evidence: lib/store.js:51-53 maps each filter entry to `${column} = ${quote(value)}`. quote() at lib/store.js:19-21 doubles single quotes, which handles the value side, but the column side is interpolated raw. The filter map arrives from routes/notifications.js:48 via the searchSchema at routes/notifications.js:22-25, which declares `additionalProperties: {type: 'string'}` — that constrains the values and places no constraint whatsoever on the property names. A body of {"filter": {"1=1 OR 1=1--": "x"}} produces WHERE 1=1 OR 1=1-- = 'x'. This is the case WEB-07 names explicitly: the parts that cannot be parameterised (table, ORDER BY column, LIMIT) admit only an allowlist, and there is none.
findings.impact: Full read of the notifications table across every tenant, and subquery-based extraction of any other table the pool's role can reach. The error handler at server.js:48 returns err.message, so a syntax error comes back verbatim, turning a blind injection into an error-based one.
findings.recommendation: Validate each column against a literal allowlist of the columns the filter UI can produce, and reject anything else with 400; bind the values with $n placeholders instead of quote(). Add propertyNames with a pattern to the JSON schema as a second layer.

triage.reason: No allowlist, no schema constraint on property names, and no database-side control. The only control on the path is quote(), which lib/store.js:19 applies to the value and never to the column.
The map is the request body at routes/notifications.js:48 (request.body.filter) and, on the unauthenticated /admin path, routes/admin.js:11.

findings.title: Notification search runs the caller's filter with no tenant predicate of its own
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: cross-tenant search (no tenant pin on /notifications/search)
findings.evidence: Every other read in this file pins the tenant server-side: routes/notifications.js:34 passes request.user.tenantId to listNotifications, and :38 passes it to getNotification, which binds it at lib/store.js:67. The search handler at :48 passes request.body.filter straight through, and lib/store.js:50-61 adds no tenant predicate of its own — where the filter is empty the WHERE clause is literally TRUE (lib/store.js:54). A signed-in member of tenant A sends {"filter": {"tenant_id": "B"}}, or an empty filter, and reads tenant B's rows. This is the sibling asymmetry WEB-24 describes, inside one file: two handlers reaching the same table, one scoped and one not.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user reads every tenant's notification subjects, recipients and delivery status, up to the 200-row page. Independent of PULSE-02: no injection is needed.
findings.recommendation: Make the tenant predicate structural — have searchNotifications take tenantId as its first parameter and always emit `tenant_id = $1 AND (...)`, so no caller can omit it. Add a two-tenant integration test as WEB-04's minimal test prescribes.

triage.reason: No mandatory scope exists: lib/store.js:50-61 issues the query with no tenant term, and there is no ORM, row-level security policy or interceptor in the tree that would add one.
The selected columns at lib/store.js:56 include recipient, which is the destination address of a message — personal data by PRV-01's standard, not public content.

findings.title: Template preview compiles a request-supplied expression with new Function
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: RCE via {{= }} new Function in template preview
findings.evidence: render.js:25 matches {{= ... }} and render.js:28 passes the captured body into `new Function(...keys, 'return (' + body + ');')`, then calls it at :29. The template string is the caller's: routes/notifications.js:58-61 takes request.body.template with no schema on that route (contrast the two routes above it, which do declare schemas) and passes String(template) into renderTemplate. The regex body is `[^}]+?`, so the expression may not contain a closing brace — that constrains the payload shape and does not prevent execution, since a call chain reaching process needs no brace. escapeHtml is applied to the return value at :29, which sanitises the output after the side effect has already run.
findings.impact: Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the API process, with the database pool and DATABASE_URL in scope. Reachable by any authenticated user.
findings.recommendation: Delete the {{= }} branch. If inline pluralisation is required, implement it as a fixed set of named helpers invoked by name with the variables as arguments, never by compiling caller text. Add a schema to the preview route.

triage.reason: The template comes from request.body at routes/notifications.js:59; the route declares no schema and the handler only coerces it with String().
new Function compiles and render.js:29 invokes the result. WEB-09's exculpation requires the data to travel as context rather than as the template; here the caller supplies the template itself.
There is no sandbox: new Function bodies run in the ambient realm with access to require via process.mainModule. escapeHtml at render.js:29 acts on the return value only.

findings.title: Delivery webhook verifies its signature only when the caller chooses to send one
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: webhook signature optional when header absent
findings.evidence: routes/webhooks.js:39 reads the signature header, and :44 wraps the entire verification — the staleness window at :45-49 and the constant-time comparison at :50-53 — in `if (header)`. Omitting the x-pulse-signature header skips all of it and execution falls through to :56. The comment at :42-43 states the intent ('only enforce the signature once the provider starts sending one'). This is WEB-27's shape exactly: the control is present, correctly written and cannot be made to reject a caller who simply does not invoke it. The route is also outside the auth scope (server.js:42), so no session compensates.
findings.impact: Anyone on the network forges delivery receipts: POST /hooks/deliveries with an array of {id, status, received_at} objects writes straight into the deliveries table via lib/store.js:85-92, whose ON CONFLICT clause overwrites the status of existing rows. Delivery state for any provider_id can be flipped, corrupting billing and retry logic.
findings.recommendation: Require the header: reject with 401 when it is absent. If unmigrated provider accounts genuinely exist, gate the exemption on an explicit per-account allowlist checked server-side, not on the presence of a header the caller controls.

triage.reason: No layer in the tree compensates: server.js:42 registers the webhook routes outside apiScope, so neither the session hook nor the rate limiter runs on them.
The branch is unconditional application code in the shipped handler, not behind a flag or a debug path.
expectedSignature at :7-14 and signatureMatches at :16-21 are both correctly implemented; the defect is solely that :44 makes reaching them optional.

findings.title: The public-path prefix /api/v1/notifications/public also matches public-digest, exposing any tenant's recipients unauthenticated
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: public-digest leaks recipients for any tenant
findings.evidence: plugins/auth.js:13-16 decides publicness with pathname.startsWith(prefix) over config/default.json:11-14, whose second entry is '/api/v1/notifications/public'. The digest route is registered at routes/notifications.js:53 as '/notifications/public-digest/:tenantId', which under the /api/v1 prefix becomes /api/v1/notifications/public-digest/... — and that string starts with the declared prefix, so plugins/auth.js:41 returns before any token is required. The handler then reads request.params.tenantId with no check and calls lib/store.js:73-83, which selects id, subject, recipient, status and created_at for whatever tenant was named.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller enumerates tenant identifiers and retrieves the 25 most recent notifications of each, including the recipient address of every one. That is cross-tenant disclosure of personal data with no credential. The prefix-matching defect is general: any future route whose name begins with 'public' inherits the same exemption.
findings.recommendation: Match public paths exactly, or require a segment boundary (path === prefix || path.startsWith(prefix + '/')), which is what edge-relay/app/deps.py:69 does correctly in the sibling service. Then authorise the digest itself with an unguessable per-recipient token rather than the tenant id.

triage.reason: The comment at routes/notifications.js:51-52 intends a link opened from a mail client, which bounds the exposure to one recipient's own messages. What ships is bounded by the tenant id instead, so the intended bound is not the enforced one and the finding moves to the enumeration.
lib/store.js:75 selects recipient — the address a message was sent to.
tenantId is a path parameter, fully caller-controlled, and lib/store.js:73 applies no other predicate.

findings.title: The rate limiter is installed only inside the API scope, leaving the webhook, admin and health surfaces unlimited
findings.class: Missing resource limit on the unauthenticated surface
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: rate limit covers only /api/v1
findings.evidence: config/default.json:15-19 declares a rateLimit block (max 300 per minute, an allowList) — a knob an operator can tune. Its only reader is plugins/ratelimit.js, registered at server.js:30 inside apiScope. The routes registered outside that scope — /admin/* (server.js:38), /hooks/* (server.js:42) and /healthz (server.js:44) — get no limiter. WEB-23 calls out this exact yield: the missing limit matters most where no credential is required, and /hooks/deliveries requires none (see PULSE-05) while writing to the database on every request.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated, unmetered writes to the deliveries table and unmetered destructive calls to /admin. The configured limit reads as coverage in the config file while covering only the authenticated routes, which are the ones least in need of it.
findings.recommendation: Register the limiter at the root instead of inside apiScope, keying on request.user?.id ?? request.ip so it degrades to an IP key where no session exists.

triage.reason: A proxy or gateway in front could limit these paths, but no such artifact is in this tree — no ingress config, no gateway definition. Per FP-08 an unevidenced external control is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS, which is why this is reported as confirmed only for the code fact and its severity kept at medium.
The registration at server.js:30 is a normal Fastify plugin registration inside an encapsulated scope; nothing else in the tree re-registers it.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: Rate-limit buckets accumulate in a Map that is only cleared on server close
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: rate-limit bucket map unbounded
findings.evidence: plugins/ratelimit.js:29 creates the Map, :41 inserts a bucket per key, and the only removal is the wholesale clear on the onClose hook at :52. Expired buckets are overwritten when the same key returns (:40-42) but never evicted otherwise, so each distinct key costs memory permanently for the process's lifetime. Keys are per-user id or per-IP (:36).
findings.impact: A caller rotating source addresses grows the map without bound; the process's memory is the only ceiling. The comment at :26-27 accepts an in-process counter deliberately, but the sweep the design implies is absent.
findings.recommendation: Sweep expired buckets on a timer, or replace the Map with a bounded LRU. The comment's stated reason for avoiding Redis does not require unbounded retention.

triage.reason: There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere; this is the only limiter in the service. It stays a low-severity availability finding on its own merits rather than an informational one.
server.js:59 binds 0.0.0.0, so the keys are supplied by remote principals.

findings.title: The error handler returns the raw exception message to the client
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: error handler leaks internal messages
findings.evidence: server.js:46-49 logs the error and then sends { error: err.message } with err.statusCode || 500. Nothing distinguishes an application error from a driver error, so a pg error — which carries the failing SQL fragment, the position and the constraint name — is returned verbatim to the caller.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance detail on the schema and the queries, and specifically an oracle that converts PULSE-02's injection from blind to error-based.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message with a correlation id for anything the application did not raise deliberately, and keep err.message in the log only, as WEB-22's exculpation describes.

triage.reason: No filter or mapping layer stands between the thrown error and the reply; server.js:48 sends err.message directly.
setErrorHandler is registered unconditionally in build(), which is the shipped entry point used at server.js:57.

findings.title: The config endpoint publishes the proxy ranges, the public-path allowlist and a token-shaped default
findings.unaided_label: pulse-notify: /admin/config discloses config + demoToken
findings.evidence: routes/admin.js:22-29 returns config.trustedProxies, config.publicPrefixes and the whole config.defaults object. config/default.json:28-32 puts a value named demoToken inside defaults. Because of PULSE-01 the endpoint answers with no credential, and path_coverage.py flagged '/config' [routes/admin.js:22] as an unguarded sibling.
findings.impact: Hands an anonymous caller the two lists that define this service's trust decisions — which network ranges are treated as proxies (feeding request.ip resolution) and exactly which prefixes skip authentication, which is the input needed to find PULSE-06 without reading the source. The demoToken value is published alongside them; whether it is inert is not established by the tree beyond its name.
findings.recommendation: Return only the version, behind the operator role. Never serialise a defaults block wholesale — enumerate the keys the console needs.

triage.reason: publicPrefixes and trustedProxies are load-bearing security configuration, not public content. Their disclosure is what makes PULSE-06 discoverable from outside.
This is an output-side disclosure; there is no attacker-controlled input to trace.

demoToken may be the inert documentation sample its name suggests, as beacon-cdk's docs.exampleApiKey demonstrably is. Nothing in this tree states so — unlike environments.ts:76, which does. The finding stands on the two configuration lists regardless; only the token half is uncertain, and the severity is set from the lists.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-09 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The nginx IP allowlist protects /internal/, a path the application does not serve; the operator surface is mounted at /ops and falls through to the catch-all
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: nginx guards /internal/ but app mounts /ops (dead guard)
findings.evidence: relay.conf:25-31 declares the only authorization in the edge config: allow 10.20.0.0/16, allow 10.30.4.0/24, deny all — scoped to location /internal/. The application's route table is app/main.py:23-30 and mounts exactly four prefixes: /healthz, /api, /ops and /p. Nothing is served under /internal. nginx picks the longest matching prefix location, so a request to /ops/flags matches location / at relay.conf:56 and is proxied with no allow/deny at all. The application then declines to re-check, by design: app/routes_admin.py:3-4 states 'the edge only forwards them from the office ranges and the jump hosts, so they do not re-check membership'. Both files are internally consistent; the guard and the thing it was meant to guard were named differently.
findings.impact: The operator API is reachable from the internet: POST /ops/flags mutates feature flags (routes_admin.py:39-43), POST /ops/replay re-delivers stored webhook payloads to a caller-named tenant (:46-55), DELETE /ops/tenants/{id} is a purge endpoint (:58-60), and GET /ops/status is EDGE-02. The one control the operator surface relies on cannot fire.
findings.recommendation: Change the location to /ops/ (and keep /internal/ only if something serves it), then stop relying on the edge alone: enforce the operator role inside routes_admin.py as well, so the control survives a future re-mount.

triage.reason: The compensating layer is precisely what is missing. app/middleware.py:43 exempts /ops/status entirely and, for the rest of /ops, checks only that a cookie is signed — never a role (see EDGE-03).
Both halves are in this repository — the nginx config at nginx/relay.conf and the mount at app/main.py:28 — so this is not a control living outside the tree. The join is decidable here.
nginx prefix-location semantics are unambiguous: /ops/... does not match location /internal/. There is no regex location, no rewrite and no map in the file that could redirect it.

findings.title: /ops/status is on the public-path list and returns the database URL, which carries the Postgres password
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: /ops/status public + leaks DATABASE_URL with password
findings.evidence: app/deps.py:11-15 lists PUBLIC_PATHS and its second entry is '/ops/status'. app/middleware.py:43-45 returns before any credential check for those paths. The route resolves to that exact string: Mount('/ops') at app/main.py:28 plus Route('/status') at app/routes_admin.py:64. The handler at routes_admin.py:26 returns settings.database_url, which deps.py:28 reads from RELAY_DATABASE_URL, which docker-compose.yml:21 sets to postgresql://relay:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/relay — a DSN with the password embedded. The response also carries template_dir and pid. This route is reachable even though EDGE-01's guard is absent, and would remain reachable even if it were present, because the exemption is inside the application.
findings.impact: Anonymous disclosure of the database username, host, port, database name and password in one unauthenticated GET. With docker-compose.yml:26-27 publishing the application port directly (EDGE-08), and the database container on the same compose network, this is a direct path to the data store.
findings.recommendation: Remove database_url, template_dir and pid from the payload — a liveness widget needs env and uptime at most. Remove '/ops/status' from PUBLIC_PATHS. Treat the password as disclosed and rotate it.

triage.reason: The exemption is the first branch of the only auth middleware (middleware.py:43), so no layer below it runs; and the edge has no allow/deny for this path (EDGE-01).
The value is a credential-bearing DSN per docker-compose.yml:21, not public content.
PUBLIC_PATHS is a module-level constant with no environment gate, and the handler has no debug branch; this is what ships.

findings.title: The operator surface authorises on a valid signature alone — any tenant's session cookie is an operator cookie, and the declared operator audience is never checked
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: no role check on /ops (any signed cookie = operator)
findings.evidence: app/middleware.py:59-65 verifies the cookie's HMAC and then assigns the decoded claims wholesale to request.state.user. No branch anywhere reads a role: grep for 'role' across edge-relay/app/ returns exactly one hit, middleware.py:51, inside the local-debug branch that ruled_out R17 shows cannot run in what ships. None of the four handlers in routes_admin.py:63-67 checks anything. Settings.operator_audience is declared at deps.py:30-32 and set in docker-compose.yml:22 — a configured knob whose only reader, routes_admin.py:27, prints it in a response rather than comparing it to anything. That is WEB-23's shape sitting on top of the authorization gap.
findings.impact: Once EDGE-01 has let the request reach the app, any principal holding a validly signed session — an ordinary tenant user of the product — has full operator rights: flag mutation, webhook replay against another tenant, and tenant purge. The from_office() call at routes_admin.py:53 is reported in the response body and gates nothing.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit check on every /ops handler comparing a role or audience claim against settings.operator_audience, and fail closed when the claim is absent. Enforce it in one place the routes cannot be registered around — a Mount-level middleware on the admin sub-application.

triage.reason: The one control on the path, SessionAuthMiddleware, establishes authenticity and not authority; middleware.py:64 copies the claims into state without inspecting them.
Tenant users and operators are different principals, and routes_admin.py:58-60 acts on a tenant named by the caller.
The sign-in service that mints the cookie is outside the tree, but that cannot supply the missing check: the claims it issues are read at middleware.py:64 and no code here branches on them.

findings.title: The edge reflects any Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while allowing credentials
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: CORS origin reflection with credentials in nginx
findings.evidence: relay.conf:39-41 emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: $http_origin, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and Vary: Origin for every response under /api/. $http_origin is the client's own header, echoed unconditionally — there is no map, no if, no allowlist anywhere in the two nginx files. The comment at :37-38 gives the reason ('the browser origin is not fixed'), which explains the reflection without bounding it. The API behind it is cookie-authenticated (middleware.py:55).
findings.impact: Any page a victim visits can read authenticated /api responses in the victim's session, because the browser attaches the relay_session cookie and the response authorises the attacker's origin to read it. GET /api/whoami returns the session claims and the resolved IP; GET /api/preview turns into a cross-origin SSRF proxy driven by the victim's browser. This is WEB-16's canonical pair: reflected origin plus credentials.
findings.recommendation: Replace the reflection with a map that echoes the Origin only when it matches the tenant-subdomain pattern exactly, anchored at both ends, and emit nothing when it does not match. Never emit a wildcard together with credentials.

triage.reason: No allowlist exists in either nginx file, and the application sets no CORS headers of its own that could override — grep for Access-Control across edge-relay returns only relay.conf:39-41.
The routes under /api are authenticated and return session claims (routes_public.py:16) and preview results, not identical public data.

findings.title: Link preview fetches any URL the caller supplies, following redirects, with no scheme or host restriction
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: SSRF in /api/preview
findings.evidence: routes_public.py:28 reads the url query parameter; the only validation is that it is non-empty (:29-30). :32-33 then issues client.get(target) with follow_redirects=True. There is no scheme check, no host allowlist, no address-family or private-range check, and no egress proxy — grep across the service finds no allowlist constant of any kind. The response is partly reflected back: status_code, the <title> text and content-type (:40-46), which gives the caller a read oracle rather than a blind one.
findings.impact: The service reaches whatever its network position reaches — the cloud metadata endpoint, the thumbs:8100 container that docker-compose.yml:34 deliberately exposes only inside the network, and the db host — and reports status, content type and title back to the caller. follow_redirects=True means an allowlist added at the entry point alone would still be defeated by a 302.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the hostname, reject non-public addresses before connecting, disable automatic redirects and re-validate on each hop, and restrict the scheme to http/https. Better, route previews through a dedicated egress proxy with its own allowlist.

triage.reason: No allowlist, no redirect handling and no network egress policy in the repository; docker-compose.yml declares no network restrictions on the app service.
target is request.query_params.get('url') at routes_public.py:28.

The route is registered unconditionally at routes_public.py:76. Preconditions: it sits behind SessionAuthMiddleware, so a validly signed cookie is required; note that docker-compose.yml sets no RELAY_SESSION_SECRET, so in that exact compose every non-public route answers 401 at middleware.py:56-57 until the secret is configured. That is an incomplete deployment, not a control.

findings.title: client_ip takes the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry, which the edge appends to rather than replacing, so from_office() is caller-controlled
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: client_ip / from_office trust X-Forwarded-For
findings.evidence: deps.py:54-56 returns forwarded.split(',')[0].strip() — the first entry — and the docstring at :51-52 states the assumption that 'the first entry is the original client'. relay.conf:16 sets X-Forwarded-For to $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for, which appends the peer to whatever the client already sent rather than overwriting it. The client therefore chooses the first entry. from_office() at deps.py:63-65 builds on it with a plain string prefix test against OFFICE_NETWORKS.
findings.impact: A caller sending X-Forwarded-For: 10.20.0.1 is reported as being inside the office network. In the shipped code the only consumer is routes_admin.py:53, which puts from_office in the replay response rather than branching on it, so the present impact is a falsified audit value rather than a bypass — but the helper is a general-purpose trust primitive and its next caller inherits the defect. The whoami response (routes_public.py:18) also echoes the spoofed value.
findings.recommendation: Take the rightmost entry the trusted hop count justifies, or read X-Real-IP, which relay.conf:15 sets from $remote_addr and which a client cannot influence, and compare with an ipaddress network membership test rather than str.startswith.

triage.reason: nginx does not strip an inbound X-Forwarded-For anywhere in relay.conf; $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for is defined to preserve and append.

The impact does reach a consumer: routes_admin.py:53 writes the spoofed verdict into the replay response and routes_public.py:18 echoes the spoofed address in whoami, so a falsified 'this came from the office' record is produced and served. It is not merely a latent defence-in-depth gap. That the value gates nothing today is why the severity is medium rather than high, not why it would be informational.
The header is request-supplied at deps.py:54.

findings.title: Session cookies are accepted on signature alone; no expiry claim is checked
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: session cookie has no expiry check
findings.evidence: _unsign at middleware.py:17-34 verifies the HMAC correctly with compare_digest and decodes the JSON payload. Neither it nor its caller at :59-64 inspects any temporal claim: grep for exp, expires, expiry and ttl across middleware.py returns nothing. The claims are assigned to request.state.user unconditionally at :64. The sibling services diverge here — pulse-notify/plugins/auth.js:28 does compare expires_at — so this is not a house convention.
findings.impact: A cookie captured once is valid for as long as the signing secret lives. There is no server-side session record to revoke either, since _unsign is self-contained, so logout and compromise response have nothing to act on.
findings.recommendation: Require an exp claim, reject when it is absent or past, and keep the window short. Add an issued-at plus a server-side revocation list if sessions must be terminable.

triage.reason: No layer expires it: the cookie is self-contained and no store is consulted anywhere in the service.

The sign-in service that mints the cookie is outside the tree and may set a Max-Age on the Set-Cookie. That bounds a compliant browser and not an attacker holding the value, so it would not exculpate; and no artifact for it arrived. Recorded as UNKNOWN, which is why this ships at medium.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The application port is published to the host, so every control implemented at the edge is optional
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: app port 8000 published, bypasses the edge
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml:26-27 publishes 8000:8000 on the app service, and the comment at :24-25 gives the reason ('so the load tester and the on-call debugger can reach the service without going through the edge container'). Everything relay.conf implements — the allow/deny at :25-31, the limit_req and limit_conn at :34-35, the client_max_body_size at :10, and the three security headers at :19-21 — lives in the edge container only. The thumbs service at :32-36 shows the correct pattern for comparison: expose, not ports.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the host on 8000 bypasses rate limiting, body-size caps, security headers and any future IP allowlist in one step. It also means fixing EDGE-01 at the nginx layer alone would not close EDGE-01's impact.
findings.recommendation: Replace ports with expose so the port stays on the compose network, and reach it for debugging through a bastion or docker exec. If a host binding is genuinely needed, bind it to 127.0.0.1:8000 rather than all interfaces.

triage.reason: FP-05 exculpates an intended, bounded exposure such as a load balancer on 443. Here the exposure is the origin itself and nothing in the repository bounds it — no host-interface binding, no firewall definition, no network policy.
A host firewall could restrict 8000, but no such artifact is in the tree. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS; the severity is set at medium for it.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The request path is written into a line-oriented log with no neutralisation, on both the access and the auth-failure path
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: log injection via request path
findings.evidence: log_escaper.py returned exit 1 with exactly two uncleared calls in the whole tree, both in this file: middleware.py:61 ('rejected session cookie for %s', path) and middleware.py:71 ('%s %s -> %s', method, path, status). No escaper sits on either path. The value is request.url.path, which is scope['path'] — percent-decoded by the ASGI server, so %0d%0a in the request target becomes a real CRLF in the string. The logger is configured with logging.basicConfig-style line output (app/main.py:16 sets only the level; no structured formatter is configured anywhere in the service), so one request produces two records. WEB-28's own note applies here: the %s idiom is what makes this read as correct, and both interpolation styles carry the same defect.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller — /healthz and /ops/status need no credential — forges arbitrary log records, including plausible successful-authentication lines, which destroys the accountability of the auth log that middleware.py:61 exists to produce. If the log is rendered in any viewer as HTML, the same input reaches that page as markup.
findings.recommendation: Escape control characters before logging, or emit one JSON object per event and confirm the consumer parses that format — WEB-28 requires both halves, not either.

triage.reason: The path is attacker-supplied and reaches the call without an allowlist or pattern check; deps.py:72 SLUG_RE constrains only the {slug} parameter of one route, not the logged path.
The sink is a line-oriented text logger: app/main.py:16 configures only the level and no structured formatter exists in the service, so a newline in the value terminates the record.
The deferred %s form is not the escaping it resembles: logging performs the interpolation itself and neutralises nothing.

findings.title: The database container is provisioned with a password written into the compose file
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: hardcoded Postgres password in the compose file
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml:43 sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD: relay_local_dev_only as a literal, in the same file that is otherwise careful to interpolate the app's copy from the environment (:21 uses ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}). The two do not agree unless the environment variable happens to hold the same literal — which means either the app cannot connect, or the deployment is run with that exact value. The file carries no dev/prod split: the app service beside it sets RELAY_ENV: production (:20), so this is the production compose.
findings.impact: The database password for a production-flagged stack is in the repository. WEB-19 is explicit that a versioned secret is compromised from the moment it was pushed, so the remediation is rotation and not editing the file.
findings.recommendation: Move the value to a secret or an env file kept out of version control, use the same ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} reference on both services so they cannot diverge, and rotate the current value.

triage.reason: This is a secret-exposure finding, not a data-flow one; there is no attacker-controlled input to trace.

The same file sets RELAY_ENV: production at :20 and restart: unless-stopped on every service, so it is not a development-only artifact. WEB-19's exculpation requires verifying that the real environment uses another source; here the sibling service on line 21 reads from the environment while this one does not.
It is the credential for the data store, whatever its entropy.

findings.title: add_header inside location /api/ discards the three security headers declared at server level
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: add_header in location resets security headers on /api/
findings.evidence: relay.conf:19-21 sets X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy at server level. nginx's add_header directives are inherited from the previous level only when the current level declares none of its own; location /api/ declares three (:39-41), so the server-level trio is not inherited there. The same applies to no other location, because no other location declares an add_header — /static/, /healthz and / all keep the inherited set.
findings.impact: API responses lose nosniff, framing protection and referrer control. Impact is modest for JSON, and matters most for any /api response a browser may render or for a future non-JSON response on that prefix.
findings.recommendation: Repeat the three server-level headers inside location /api/, or move all of them into an included snippet referenced from every location.

triage.reason: There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere in the tree — the application sets no security headers of its own; grep across edge-relay/app finds none. It stays a low-severity defence-in-depth gap rather than dropping to informational.
nginx add_header inheritance is level-based and documented; the presence of any add_header at the location level is what cancels inheritance, and three are present.

findings.title: State-changing operator endpoints are authorised by an ambient cookie with no anti-CSRF token
findings.unaided_label: edge-relay: CSRF on /ops/flags (no token)
findings.evidence: Authorization for /ops comes solely from the relay_session cookie (middleware.py:55), a credential the browser attaches on its own. There is no CSRF token anywhere in the service — grep for csrf across edge-relay returns nothing — and no custom-header requirement. POST /ops/flags (routes_admin.py:65) parses its body with request.json(), which Starlette does regardless of Content-Type, so a cross-origin form submitted with enctype=text/plain can deliver a body that parses as JSON and is therefore a simple request with no preflight to block it. POST /ops/replay (:66) is the same shape.
findings.impact: An operator who loads an attacker's page while signed in silently flips feature flags or triggers a webhook replay against a tenant the attacker names.
findings.recommendation: Require a token bound to the session on every unsafe method, or require a custom header that forces a preflight and reject requests without it. Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on the cookie at the sign-in service.

triage.reason: No token layer exists in the service, and relay.conf's CORS reflection is scoped to /api/ (:33) so it neither helps nor hinders /ops.

The SameSite attribute is set by the sign-in service, which is outside this tree; SameSite=Lax would block the cross-site POST and rule this out. Per the triage contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, and it is reported as probable for exactly that reason. DELETE /ops/tenants/{id} is separately protected by the preflight its method forces.

findings.title: The maintenance-token guard tests for /internal while the blueprint is mounted at /api/internal, so it never fires and the endpoints are wholly unauthenticated
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: enforce_internal_token prefix mismatch → internal endpoints unguarded
findings.evidence: auth.py:13 sets INTERNAL_PREFIX = "/internal" and auth.py:55 returns early unless request.path.startswith(INTERNAL_PREFIX). app.py:35 registers internal_bp with url_prefix="/api/internal", so request.path is /api/internal/status, /api/internal/import and so on — none of which start with /internal. The guard's body (auth.py:58-61, which aborts 403 when the shared header is absent or wrong) is therefore unreachable for every route it was written for. Nothing else covers them: internal.py declares no before_request, and unlike blueprints/api.py:16, which calls api_bp.before_request(require_session), the internal blueprint has no session requirement at all. path_coverage.py flagged '/import' and '/reindex' [internal.py:24,42] as unguarded siblings. Both files are individually correct; the prefix and the mount were written apart.
findings.impact: Four unauthenticated endpoints: GET /api/internal/status returns SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI (internal.py:18), which config.py:18 shows is a DSN that may carry credentials, plus IMPORT_ROOT and the debug flag; DELETE /api/internal/tenants/<id> deletes every posting of any tenant (internal.py:51) — destructive, with no credential; POST /api/internal/import runs a bulk import into a caller-named tenant (internal.py:33-38, and see LEDGER-04); POST /api/internal/reindex is unmetered database work.
findings.recommendation: Derive the guard from the registered prefix rather than restating it — compare against the blueprint's url_prefix, or better, attach enforce_internal_token as internal_bp.before_request so the two cannot drift. Add require_session to internal_bp as well, and add a test asserting 403 on every internal route with no header.

triage.reason: The only two before_request hooks are registered at app.py:28 and app.py:31; the first only populates g.user and never rejects, and the second is the one that cannot fire. No other layer exists in the tree.
Both halves are in this repository — auth.py:13 and app.py:35 — so the join is decidable here and does not depend on an external artifact.

internal.py:1 calls these 'endpoints driven by the ops runbooks', implying network segmentation, but nothing in the repository bounds the exposure: app.py:54 binds 127.0.0.1 only in the __main__ development path, and no proxy, ingress or firewall definition ships with the service.

findings.title: Draft restore unpickles a base64 blob taken straight from the request form
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: pickle.loads RCE on /drafts/restore
findings.evidence: api.py:78 reads request.form['state'] and api.py:79 passes base64.b64decode of it to pickle.loads. There is no signature, no HMAC, no allowlist and no type restriction — the docstring at :73-77 explains the value is stashed in the browser's local storage, which places it entirely under the client's control. WEB-11 names this sink first and notes CWE-502 is among the three worst-detected classes for SAST.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution in the application process as soon as any authenticated user posts a crafted blob; pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes during reconstruction. The process holds the database session and the config, including SECRET_KEY (LEDGER-05).
findings.recommendation: Serialise drafts as JSON and rebuild a declared DTO from it. If a binary round-trip is unavoidable, HMAC the blob with a server key and verify before deserialising — but the value here is client-authored, so JSON with a schema is the right answer.

triage.reason: The blob is request.form.get('state') at api.py:78 — the request body.
pickle.loads reconstructs arbitrary types and executes __reduce__ during load; it is not a parsing-only format.

The only control on the path is api_bp.before_request(require_session) at api.py:16, which requires a session and constrains nothing about the blob. WEB-11's exculpation requires integrity verification before deserialising; there is none.

findings.title: The reports blueprint has no session guard and falls back to a tenant named in the query string
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: reports blueprint has no session guard + tenant from query
findings.evidence: blueprints/api.py:16 registers api_bp.before_request(require_session); blueprints/reports.py registers no equivalent, and app.py:34 mounts it with no guard either. current_tenant() at auth.py:86-95 returns user['tenant_id'] when a user exists and otherwise request.args.get('tenant'). Since load_session (app.py:28) sets g.user = None for an anonymous caller rather than rejecting, all three report views resolve the tenant from the query string: reports.py:50, :72 and :91. The docstring at auth.py:88-90 states the intent — the nightly export job runs without a cookie — so the fallback exists for a batch process and is reachable by anyone. path_coverage.py flagged '/statement', '/export.csv' and '/trial-balance' [reports.py:48,70,89] as unguarded siblings of guarded paths. This is WEB-24's asymmetry across two sibling blueprints of one application.
findings.impact: GET /reports/statement?tenant=X, /reports/export.csv?tenant=X and /reports/trial-balance?tenant=X return any tenant's ledger to an anonymous caller — up to 100,000 postings per request from reports.py:79 and :96, with entry ids, account codes, amounts and memos. This is the accounting data of the whole platform, readable by tenant-id enumeration.
findings.recommendation: Add reports_bp.before_request(require_session). Give the nightly job its own authenticated service identity instead of an anonymous query-string fallback, and delete the fallback branch at auth.py:95 so a missing session can never resolve to a tenant.

triage.reason: load_session at app.py:28 is the only hook covering this blueprint and it never aborts — auth.py:20-50 has no reject path, it only populates g.user.
The data is a tenant's general ledger: entry ids, account codes, debit and credit amounts and free-text memos (reports.py:78-80).

The docstring at reports.py:3-4 says these views are also fetched by a spreadsheet add-in, which is an argument for wide client reach, not for anonymous access. Nothing bounds who may supply the tenant parameter.

findings.title: The bulk importer writes postings without Posting.clean(), so unsanitised memos reach a Markup() call in the rendered statement
findings.class: Stored cross-site scripting via a bypassed model invariant
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: stored XSS via Markup(memo) + importer bypassing clean()
findings.evidence: models.py:60-66 documents an invariant in its own docstring — 'Every posting that lands in postings must satisfy this' — and clean() enforces it: the account-code shape at :67, the debit/credit exclusivity at :74, and bleach.clean on the memo at :77-79. Two write paths honour it (services/postings.py:17 and :47). The third does not: importer.py:82 calls db.session.bulk_insert_mappings(Posting, mappings), which inserts dictionaries without instantiating the model, so clean() never runs on the rows built at importer.py:67-77 from raw CSV fields. The consumer trusts the invariant: reports.py:64 wraps the memo in Markup() — explicitly disabling Jinja's autoescaping, with the comment at :62-63 explaining that memos keep their inline formatting — and reports.py:67 renders it. A memo arriving through the import path therefore reaches the page as markup.
findings.impact: Script execution in the browser of anyone viewing /reports/statement for the affected tenant, in a financial application. The same bypass also admits malformed account codes and postings that are simultaneously debit and credit, so the ledger's balance invariant is unenforced on the bulk path.
findings.recommendation: Build Posting objects and call clean() in the import loop, or apply bleach.clean and the account-code check to each mapping before bulk_insert_mappings. Independently, stop trusting the store: sanitise at render time in reports.py:64 rather than relying on a write-time invariant that one of three writers skips.

triage.reason: The compensating control is exactly the one bypassed. bleach.clean at models.py:77 is reached only through clean(), whose callers are services/postings.py:17 and :47; bulk_insert_mappings does not invoke ORM instance methods or validators.
Markup at reports.py:64 marks the string as already-safe, so render_template_string emits it unescaped into the <td> at :30.

The memo originates in a CSV staged on the import volume, described at importer.py:2 as dropped by banks. Whether an attacker can influence that file's contents is not established by this tree — LEDGER-01 lets anyone name which staged file to import and under which tenant, but not author it. Per the triage contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed. The invariant bypass itself is confirmed by reading importer.py:82.

findings.title: The production config falls back to a hardcoded SECRET_KEY when the environment variable is absent
findings.class: Hardcoded cryptographic key with fail-open default
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: hardcoded default SECRET_KEY
findings.evidence: config.py:15 reads os.environ.get("LEDGER_SECRET_KEY", "ledger-flow-default-secret") — a two-argument get, so a missing variable yields the literal rather than raising. The comment at :14 states what the key does: 'Signs the session cookie and the CSRF tokens.' The fallback lives in BaseConfig, which ProductionConfig inherits (:38), and load() at :49-52 defaults to ProductionConfig for any unrecognised name. Nothing anywhere in the service asserts the variable is set: grep for LEDGER_SECRET_KEY returns only this line. The confirmed defect is the fail-open — a production configuration that boots with a key printed in the repository instead of refusing to start.
findings.impact: Where the variable is unset, anyone reading this file can forge a Flask session cookie setting session['uid'] to any user id, which auth.py:24-34 turns into a fully populated g.user with that user's role and tenant. That is complete authentication bypass and privilege escalation. Independently, the literal is now a published string and must be treated as compromised wherever it was ever used.
findings.recommendation: Raise on a missing LEDGER_SECRET_KEY in ProductionConfig rather than defaulting — fail closed, as storage.js:28 does correctly in the sibling orchard-jobs service. Rotate the current key, which invalidates existing sessions by design.

triage.reason: The fallback is not on a debug-only branch: it is a class attribute of BaseConfig, inherited by ProductionConfig at config.py:38, and load() returns ProductionConfig for any unknown or missing LEDGER_CONFIG value (:50-52). TestingConfig overrides the database URI and the CSRF flag but not this key.
The key value is a literal in the repository, so it is known to any reader; the attacker-controlled part is the cookie they forge with it.

A deployment outside the tree may well set LEDGER_SECRET_KEY, which would mean no live forgery today. No such artifact arrived, and per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. It does not change the confirmed defect, which is the fail-open default and the versioned literal; it is why the impact is stated conditionally.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: CSV export writes cell values verbatim, so a memo beginning with = is a formula in the consuming spreadsheet
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: CSV formula injection in export.csv
findings.evidence: reports.py:80 writes entry_id, account_code, debit, credit and memo straight into csv.writer with no neutralisation of a leading =, +, - or @. The memo is user-authored on both write paths: services/postings.py:15 takes it from the request body, and bleach.clean at models.py:77 strips HTML tags but leaves plain text such as =HYPERLINK(...) entirely intact — the sanitiser is the right one for the HTML sink and the wrong one for this sink. The consumer is stated at reports.py:3-4: 'the accountants' spreadsheet add-in'.
findings.impact: A posting memo crafted by any user of a tenant executes as a formula when an accountant opens the export, which is the documented path for data exfiltration to a remote URL or, with the spreadsheet's own confirmation prompt, command execution on the accountant's workstation.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is =, +, - , @, tab or carriage return with a single quote, or quote every field and set the export's content type so the consumer treats it as text.

triage.reason: bleach.clean at models.py:77 is the only transformation applied, and it targets HTML tags; a leading = is not a tag and passes through untouched.
The memo reaches the row from the request body via services/postings.py:15, and from CSV import via importer.py:74.
The victim is the accountant opening the file, a different principal from the tenant user who wrote the memo.

findings.title: The export's Content-Disposition filename is interpolated from an unvalidated query parameter
findings.unaided_label: ledger-flow: Content-Disposition filename injection from tenant param
findings.evidence: reports.py:85 builds f'attachment; filename="{tenant}.csv"' where tenant comes from current_tenant(), which for an anonymous caller is request.args.get('tenant') (auth.py:95) with no pattern check anywhere on that path. A value containing a double quote closes the quoted-string and lets the caller append further Content-Disposition parameters; a value containing a path separator or a semicolon manipulates the suggested filename.
findings.impact: Control over the filename the browser saves, which can be used to suggest a misleading or double-extension name, and control over additional header parameters within Content-Disposition.
findings.recommendation: Validate the tenant against the same pattern the model uses, or percent-encode the filename with a filename* parameter per RFC 6266 rather than interpolating.

triage.reason: The value is request.args.get('tenant') via auth.py:95; no validation stands between it and the f-string.

Modern Werkzeug rejects header values containing CR or LF, which removes the response-splitting half of this class; the exact version is not pinned in this tree — there is no requirements file — so the residual is the quote-breaking half, which no version blocks. That UNKNOWN caps this at probable and is also why the severity is low rather than medium.

findings.title: The session middleware falls back to a legacy parser that decodes the JWT payload without verifying any signature
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: ParseLegacy unsigned-token fallback = auth bypass
findings.evidence: token.go:36-62 is a correct verifier: it pins the method to HMAC, passes jwt.WithValidMethods([]string{"HS256"}) and jwt.WithExpirationRequired, and checks tok.Valid. ParseLegacy at token.go:67-87 is not a verifier at all — it splits on '.', base64-decodes parts[1], json.Unmarshals it into Claims, and checks only that Subject is non-empty and that Expires, if present, is in the future. The signature segment is never read and the secret is never touched. middleware/auth.go:51-61 calls Parse first and, on any error, calls ParseLegacy and accepts its result. Because Parse fails for a forged token, the fallback is reached by every forged token. The claims then populate Scope wholesale at auth.go:63-68, including Role and TenantID. grep confirms auth.go:56 is ParseLegacy's only caller.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a session. `base64url({"sub":"<victim>","did":"<any device>","tid":"<any tenant>","role":"admin","exp":<future>}) ` placed between two arbitrary segments authenticates as any user, in any tenant, with any role. That subsumes every authorization control in the service and makes ATLAS-06's injection and the whole /v1 surface reachable by an anonymous caller.
findings.recommendation: Delete ParseLegacy. If handsets holding v1 envelopes must survive, verify those tokens against the v1 signing key with a real HMAC check rather than skipping verification, and put a hard end date on the path.

triage.reason: RequireSession is the only authentication layer in the service and it is the layer that accepts the unverified claims. No gateway or proxy configuration ships with atlas-sync.

WEB-01's exculpation for an unverified decode is that it feeds only logs or metrics while authorization comes from a server-side session. Here the decoded claims become the Scope at auth.go:63-68 and are the sole basis for every access decision, e.g. handlers/device.go:27 and handlers/sync.go:117.
The fallback is unconditional application code in the shipped middleware — no build tag, no environment flag, no feature check.

findings.title: The /v1/sync routes are mounted on the root router, outside the group that installs RequireSession
findings.class: Missing authentication on a route group
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: /v1/sync/* group registered outside the session group
findings.evidence: router.go:40-49 opens r.Group, adds RequireSession and PerUserRateLimit to that inline sub-router, and registers /v1/profile, /v1/devices, /v1/devices/import and /v1/records inside it. router.go:53-60 then calls r.Route("/v1/sync", ...) on the root router r, and the only middleware it adds is a Timeout and MaxBytes. chi's Group applies its middleware to the routes declared inside that closure; a sibling mounted on r afterwards inherits only what was registered on r before any route — RequestID, RealIP, Recoverer, SecurityHeaders and Timeout (router.go:27-31), none of which authenticate. The comment at router.go:51-52 explains why sync got its own scope (a longer timeout and a body cap) and shows the session requirement was lost in the move. path_coverage.py flagged '/delta', '/push' and '/attachment' [router.go:57-59] as unguarded siblings.
findings.impact: GET /v1/sync/delta, POST /v1/sync/push and GET /v1/sync/attachment answer with no credential at all. Combined with ATLAS-04 the delta stream returns any device's records to an anonymous caller and push writes into any device's account; with ATLAS-03 the attachment handler is an anonymous arbitrary-file read.
findings.recommendation: Register the sync routes inside the authenticated group, using a nested r.Route within the Group closure so the per-route timeout and body cap are preserved, and add a router test asserting 401 for every route outside the small public allowlist.

triage.reason: No handler in the sync group re-checks: handlers/sync.go:47, :78 and :127 read the scope or the query directly and none rejects an empty Scope.
main.go:69 binds :8080 on all interfaces and nothing in the repository restricts who reaches these paths.
chi's Group and Route semantics are unambiguous: Group's middleware stack is local to the closure, and r.Route mounts a fresh sub-router carrying only the root's pre-route middleware.

findings.title: The attachment handler joins a caller-supplied name onto the storage directory with no containment check
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: path traversal in Attachment
findings.evidence: sync.go:128 reads the name query parameter; the only check is that it is non-empty (:129-132). sync.go:134 then calls os.Open(filepath.Join(h.attachDir, name)). filepath.Join calls Clean on the result, which resolves .. segments rather than rejecting them, so Join("/var/att", "../../etc/passwd") yields /etc/passwd. There is no filepath.Rel check, no strings.HasPrefix against the base, no allowlist and no UUID scheme — the comment at :125-126 asserts 'The names are opaque identifiers generated by the client SDK', which is a statement about the honest client and not a control. The contrast is instructive: ledger-flow/services/importer.py:27-29 does exactly the canonicalisation this handler omits.
findings.impact: Arbitrary file read from the service's filesystem, returned as application/octet-stream. Because the route sits in the unauthenticated sync group (ATLAS-02), no credential is needed — configuration, key material and /proc contents are all in reach.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the joined path with filepath.EvalSymlinks and require filepath.Rel(base, resolved) to produce a path that neither starts with '..' nor is absolute, before opening. Reject any name containing a separator outright.

triage.reason: name is r.URL.Query().Get("name") at sync.go:128 with no validation between there and the Join.
os.Open followed by io.Copy at :142 streams whatever the resolved path points at; nothing constrains the type or location.
WEB-12's exculpation requires a server-generated name or a canonical path verified against the base. Neither is present; ATLAS_ATTACHMENT_DIR (main.go:63) only sets the base.

findings.title: resolveDevice accepts a device id from the query string whenever the token does not carry one
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: resolveDevice falls back to query device_id → IDOR
findings.evidence: sync.go:39-44 returns the scope's DeviceID when it is non-empty and otherwise r.URL.Query().Get("device_id"), with no check that the named device belongs to the caller. The docstring at :36-38 gives the reason (handsets before 3.2 do not carry the device in the token). Both consumers use it as the authorization key: Delta at :48 passes it to RecordsForDevice, whose query at store/queries.go:149 filters on device_id alone with no owner predicate; Push at :79 passes it to OwnerOfDevice at :95, which derives the owner from the device rather than from the caller, so the caller's identity plays no part in the write.
findings.impact: Reading another user's records is a query-string edit. Because the sync group is unauthenticated (ATLAS-02) the scope is always empty there, so the fallback is not an edge case on those routes — it is the only path. Push additionally writes records into whatever account owns the named device.
findings.recommendation: Require the device to come from the verified token, and where the legacy parameter must be honoured, look up the device and assert its user_id equals the caller's before using it. store.OwnerOfDevice already returns the value needed for that comparison.

triage.reason: The fallback is unconditional; there is no version check, flag or sunset gate around sync.go:43.

No query in the path scopes by owner: store/queries.go:145-152 filters on device_id and updated_at only, and queries.go:109-118 takes the owner as a parameter derived from the device rather than from the session.
Records carry a free-form Body (store/queries.go:45) belonging to another account.

findings.title: Device import persists records with the owner id supplied in the request body
findings.class: Authorization checked on the caller, not on the objects named in the body
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: Import writes records with attacker-chosen owner_id
findings.evidence: Every sibling handler in this file binds the effect to the verified scope: Profile uses scope.UserID (device.go:27), List uses it (:45), Register uses it (:67). Import does not — it does not even call ScopeFrom. device.go:82-91 decodes the body into []store.Record and passes the slice unchanged to BulkInsertRecords, which at store/queries.go:138 binds rec.OwnerID and rec.DeviceID from the wire straight into the insert. The docstring at device.go:79-80 states the intent: 'Each record keeps the owner it was exported with so a restore lands where it belongs.' The upsert clause differs from the single-record path in the same file: UpsertRecord at queries.go:115 carries `WHERE records.owner_id = $2`, and the bulk statement at queries.go:131 drops that predicate, so an existing row's body can be overwritten regardless of owner.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller — and, via ATLAS-01, any caller at all — writes records into any other user's account and overwrites existing records belonging to anyone, by id. That is cross-tenant data injection and tampering in one request.
findings.recommendation: Overwrite OwnerID with scope.UserID for every record before inserting, and restore the `WHERE records.owner_id = $2` predicate on the bulk upsert so a conflicting id cannot cross an ownership boundary.

triage.reason: OwnerID is a JSON field of the request body: store/queries.go:42 tags it `json:"owner_id"` and device.go:83 decodes the body directly into it.

RequireSession at router.go:41 authenticates the caller and constrains nothing about the ids in the body — which is precisely the WEB-25 shape. No ORM scope or database policy exists to add the predicate.
The named rows are other users' records, and naming one overwrites its body (queries.go:131).

findings.title: The activity feed interpolates a query-string value into the ORDER BY clause
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: SQLi in ListRecords ORDER BY sort param
findings.evidence: queries.go:163-168 builds the statement with fmt.Sprintf and places sortColumn into `ORDER BY %s DESC`. The value arrives from handlers/sync.go:113, r.URL.Query().Get("sort"), which is defaulted when empty (:114-116) and otherwise passed through unvalidated. The owner is bound correctly as $1, which is what makes the line read as safe. WEB-07 names this exact position: ORDER BY cannot be parameterised, so the only valid control there is an allowlist, and none exists. The comment at queries.go:160-161 ('the column to sort on comes from the segmented control') describes the honest client.
findings.impact: Boolean and error-based extraction of arbitrary data from the database through subqueries and CASE expressions in the sort position — the parameterised owner predicate does not constrain what the ORDER BY expression may read. Reachable at GET /v1/records, and via ATLAS-01 without valid credentials.
findings.recommendation: Map the segmented control's values to a fixed set of column literals and reject anything not in it; keep the allowlist in the store package so no caller can widen it. Do the same for the LIMIT construction at queries.go:88 even though its caller currently bounds it.

triage.reason: sortColumn is handlers/sync.go:113, the raw query parameter; the only transformation is the empty-string default at :114.
No allowlist, enum or column-name validation exists on the path — grep across atlas-sync finds no set of permitted sort columns anywhere.

lib/pq sends this through the extended protocol because a parameter is present, which blocks stacked statements but not the injection itself: the ORDER BY expression is still attacker-authored SQL evaluated by the server.

findings.title: The credential endpoints are registered outside the group carrying the rate limiter
findings.unaided_label: atlas-sync: no rate limit on /auth/token (brute force)
findings.evidence: PerUserRateLimit is added once, at router.go:42, inside the authenticated group. POST /auth/token and POST /auth/refresh are registered on the root router at router.go:63-64, as are /healthz (:33) and /hooks/billing (:37), so none of them is limited. The comment at :62 correctly observes that credential endpoints cannot require a session; it does not follow that they cannot be limited. IssueToken at handlers/device.go:104-119 performs a bcrypt comparison per request with no attempt counter, lockout or backoff anywhere in the service.
findings.impact: Unlimited online password guessing against every account, and unlimited bcrypt work factor consumption as a side effect — each request costs the server a full bcrypt round, so the endpoint doubles as a cheap CPU-exhaustion vector.
findings.recommendation: Apply a limiter keyed on the submitted email and on the peer address to /auth/*, with lockout bound to the identity rather than only the address, as WEB-03's exculpation requires. Note that the limiter's IP fallback (middleware/ratelimit.go:25) reads RemoteAddr, which chimw.RealIP at router.go:28 lets a caller set, so the identity key must carry the weight.

triage.reason: No lockout, counter or delay exists: handlers/device.go:104-132 has no attempt tracking and store/queries.go has no failed-login table.

An edge or WAF could throttle /auth, but atlas-sync ships no proxy configuration at all — no compose file, no ingress. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS, and it is why the severity is medium rather than high.
The endpoint performs a real credential check (bcrypt at device.go:116), so repeated calls are a functioning guessing oracle rather than an inert one.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: Job retry merges the raw request body over already-validated job data, defeating every check the submit path applies
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: retry merges unvalidated overrides (mass assignment)
findings.evidence: The submit path validates: routes.js:18 calls schema.validateRenderJob(body), which enforces the documentId pattern, the template enum, the width bounds and the asset-host allowlist (schema.js:22-28, 74-81), and routes.js:22-23 then overwrites tenantId and requestedBy from the session so the caller cannot choose them. The retry path does none of it: routes.js:55 takes ctx.request.body as `overrides` and routes.js:57 spreads it over previous.data — `{ ...previous.data, ...overrides, retryOf }` — with the caller's keys winning. Nothing between the body and the queue calls validateRenderJob. The ownership check at routes.js:51 confirms the caller owns the *original* job and says nothing about the fields they then replace. This is WEB-24's asymmetry: two sibling handlers reaching the same effect, one gated and one not.
findings.impact: Every constraint the submit path enforces is optional on retry. Overriding assetBaseUrl escapes the ASSET_HOSTS allowlist and drives ORCH-02's SSRF; overriding documentId escapes the 24-hex pattern and drives ORCH-03's arbitrary write; overriding tenantId writes the rendered artifact under another tenant's prefix (render.js:64) and, since routes.js:35 authorises reads by comparing job.data.tenantId, also detaches the job from its owner's view.
findings.recommendation: Pass the merged object through schema.validateRenderJob before enqueuing, and re-apply tenantId and requestedBy from ctx.state.user after the merge so they cannot be overridden. Better, accept an explicit allowlist of retryable fields rather than an open spread.

triage.reason: No layer revalidates: queue.enqueueRender (src/queue/index.js:39) calls Queue.add with the data as given, and the processors treat the payload as trusted — export.js:29-30 says so explicitly.
overrides is ctx.request.body at routes.js:55, parsed by bodyParser with no schema.
The tenantId override crosses a tenant boundary, and the worker runs as a separate process with filesystem and network reach the API caller does not have.

findings.title: The render worker fetches an asset manifest from a base URL carried in the job payload
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: SSRF via assetBaseUrl in worker fetch
findings.evidence: render.js:50 takes job.data.assetBaseUrl, defaulting to a constant only when absent, and render.js:21 fetches `${baseUrl}/manifest.json`. The worker performs no host check of its own — the allowlist lives at the API boundary, schema.js:74-81, and applies only to the submit path. ORCH-01 shows the retry path delivers an arbitrary assetBaseUrl into job.data untouched. The result is then interpolated into the page at render.js:57 as a stylesheet href, which headless Chromium fetches as a second request the same URL controls.
findings.impact: The worker issues attacker-directed requests from its own network position — cloud metadata, internal services, any host reachable from the worker subnet — and, through the stylesheet href, a second request whose response influences the rendered PDF. The manifest's parsed JSON is also trusted: manifest.css is placed into the HTML at render.js:57 with no escaping, so a controlled manifest injects markup into the page Chromium renders.
findings.recommendation: Re-check the host against ASSET_HOSTS inside the processor rather than only at submission — the worker is the place the request is actually made — and resolve the address to reject private ranges. Escape manifest.css before interpolating it.

triage.reason: The allowlist at schema.js:76 is on the API's submit path only; ORCH-01 is a documented route around it, and no egress proxy or network policy ships with the service.
baseUrl is job.data.assetBaseUrl (render.js:50), which the retry body sets directly.
fetch performs the request and render.js:24-27 returns the parsed body, so the caller gets both the side effect and a partial oracle through the thrown status.

findings.title: The render worker builds the working file path from documentId, which the retry path leaves unvalidated
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: arbitrary file write via documentId override
findings.evidence: render.js:54 computes path.join(workdir, `${documentId}.html`) and render.js:55 writes to it; render.js:31 derives the PDF path from the same value, and render.js:64 builds the S3 key `${tenantId}/renders/${documentId}.pdf` from it. documentId is constrained to ^[a-f0-9]{24}$ at schema.js:22 — but only on the submit path, and ORCH-01 shows the retry body overrides it with no validation at all. path.join normalises rather than rejecting, so a value containing ../ escapes the mkdtemp directory.
findings.impact: Writing attacker-chosen HTML to an arbitrary path the worker process can reach, followed by Chromium opening it as file:// (render.js:38). On a worker that also reads configuration or scripts from disk this is a direct route to code execution; at minimum it is arbitrary file overwrite. The same value poisons the S3 key at render.js:64, letting the artifact land under a path of the caller's choosing.
findings.recommendation: Validate documentId inside the processor against the same pattern the schema declares, before it is used in any path or key. Treat the queue payload as untrusted input at the point of use rather than relying on the submitter's validation — the comment at export.js:29-30 that assumes otherwise is the assumption to remove.

triage.reason: documentId reaches job.data unvalidated through routes.js:57; the schema at schema.js:22 governs only routes.js:18.
There is no canonicalisation between the value and the write: render.js:53-55 creates the temp dir, joins and writes with no Rel or prefix check.
The worker is a separate process (package.json:9, start:worker) with its own filesystem, written to on behalf of a remote API caller.

findings.title: The partner webhook enqueues export jobs without the schema validation its sibling route applies
findings.class: Validation gate one sibling enforces and the other does not
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: webhook export path bypasses schema validation
findings.evidence: The two entry points to the export queue reach the identical effect. routes.js:66-70 calls schema.validateExportJob, which enforces the tenantId pattern ^[a-z0-9-]{3,40}$ (schema.js:35), the format enum, the rows bound and — through checkFilename at schema.js:87 — the FILENAME_SEGMENTS pattern and the 128-character cap. webhook.js:47-53 constructs the same job object by hand and calls queue.enqueueExport directly, with tenantId taken raw from body.tenant_id and filename raw from body.filename. Neither validateExportJob nor checkFilename appears anywhere in webhook.js. path_coverage.py flagged '/hooks' [webhook.js:8] as an unguarded sibling.
findings.impact: Both values flow to the sink in ORCH-05, where they are joined into a filesystem path — so a partner callback can direct the worker's write outside the export root, and can name any tenant's export directory. It also allows the row cap to be exceeded, since Number(body.rows) at webhook.js:51 has no maximum where the schema declares 1000000.
findings.recommendation: Route the webhook payload through schema.validateExportJob exactly as routes.js:66 does — one validator, both callers — so the two paths cannot diverge again. Preconditions worth stating: the route is HMAC-verified at webhook.js:44, so this is reachable by a partner holding a valid signing secret rather than by an anonymous caller.

triage.reason: verifySignature at webhook.js:17-39 authenticates the partner and validates nothing about the body's contents; no other layer stands between webhook.js:47 and the queue.
tenantId and filename are body fields at webhook.js:49-50, reaching the queue unaltered.
The signature bounds *who* may call, not what they may send. A partner is a separate principal from the tenants whose directories the values address, so the boundary is still crossed.

findings.title: The export processor joins tenantId and filename into a filesystem path with no containment check
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: export processor path join without containment
findings.evidence: export.js:40 computes path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, `${filename}.${format}`), then :41 creates the parent directory recursively and :42 writes the file. Neither value is checked here — the comment at export.js:29-30 states the reason: 'Job payloads reach this queue already validated at submission time, so the processor concentrates on the conversion itself.' ORCH-04 shows one of the two producers does not validate, which makes that comment the assumption that carries the defect. loadRows at export.js:17 joins tenantId a second time, so a traversing tenant id also redirects the read.
findings.impact: A file written at an attacker-chosen path with attacker-influenced contents, as the worker user, with mkdir -p creating any missing directories along the way. The serialised payload is caller-influenced through the staged rows, so this is not limited to an empty file.
findings.recommendation: Validate both components inside the processor against the patterns schema.js already defines, and assert that path.resolve(target) starts with path.resolve(EXPORT_ROOT) + path.sep before writing. Keep the check at the sink, not only at the producers.

triage.reason: The claimed control is submission-time validation, and ORCH-04 shows the webhook producer omits it. WEB-12 requires a canonical path verified against the base before opening; export.js:40-42 performs none.
Both components originate in a request body via webhook.js:49-50.
path.join normalises .. rather than rejecting it, so the join is not the containment it resembles.
