findings.title: Rendered customer documents are uploaded with a public-read ACL and a guessable key
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: render artifacts uploaded public-read
findings.evidence: render.js:68-71 calls storage.putObject with public: true, which storage.js:39-40 turns into ACL 'public-read' and CacheControl 'public, max-age=31536000'. The key is deterministic: `${tenantId}/renders/${documentId}.pdf` (render.js:64), where documentId is a 24-hex identifier the caller supplies. The documents are invoices, statements and letters (schema.js:23), and the comment at render.js:66-67 gives the reason: the artifact is linked from customer e-mail and needs 'an address that does not expire'. render.js:75 returns storage.publicUrl(key), so the anonymous URL is what the API hands back at routes.js:42.
findings.impact: Every rendered invoice and statement is readable by anyone who has or guesses the URL, with a one-year cache lifetime and no expiry. Enumeration is bounded only by the 96-bit document id, but the URLs are distributed by e-mail and returned by the API, so they leak through referrer headers, forwarded mail and browser history without any guessing.
findings.recommendation: Upload privately and serve through a genuine time-limited link — a real presigned URL from the SDK, which is what ORCH-07 shows the homegrown mechanism is not. If a durable address is required, put a signed-cookie CDN in front of a private bucket.

triage.reason: INF-02's exculpation is a public-assets bucket with no regulated data. This is the opposite case its own text warns about — the bucket receives rendered financial documents, so the intended public-asset exposure has been extended to tenant data.
The objects are per-tenant invoices and statements, personal and financial records by PRV-01's standard.
No bucket policy or block-public-access setting in this service overrides the ACL; storage.js:32-43 is the only writer and it sets the ACL directly.

findings.title: Artifact URL signing is decorative: nothing verifies it, and the MAC is a secret-prefix SHA-256 rather than an HMAC
findings.class: Control that is present without working
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: signedUrl is decorative (never verified) + SHA length extension
findings.evidence: Two defects in one mechanism. First, nothing checks it: signedUrl (storage.js:59-63) appends ?expires=&sig= to PUBLIC_BASE, which storage.js:7-8 shows is the S3 endpoint itself — a store that ignores unknown query parameters. verifySignedUrl exists at storage.js:65-71 and grep returns zero callers anywhere in the tree, so no request path ever evaluates it. The 'time-limited link' handed out at routes.js:76-80 expires only in its own text. Second, objectSignature at storage.js:51-56 hashes `secret || key || expiresAt` with a bare SHA-256, a Merkle-Damgard construction vulnerable to length extension, where HMAC is the correct primitive — and the file already imports crypto and uses createHmac correctly elsewhere in the service (server.js:20).
findings.impact: Access to an artifact is governed entirely by the object's own ACL, which ORCH-06 shows is public-read — so the signature and TTL protect nothing at all today, while reading as a control in review and in the API response. Where a future object is private, the signature would still be forgeable by extension.
findings.recommendation: Use the SDK's getSignedUrl, which produces a signature S3 actually enforces. If a custom scheme is kept, verify it in a request path that can deny, and build the MAC with createHmac rather than a hash over a concatenated secret.

triage.reason: There is no enforcing layer: the URL points at PUBLIC_BASE (storage.js:62) and no application handler mediates artifact reads — routes.js:80 returns the URL and the browser goes straight to the store.
signedUrl is called from the shipped route at routes.js:76; it is verifySignedUrl, the half that could deny, which is absent from every path.

WEB-27 is explicit that a failed control is never filed as hardening, because the project already believes it holds it — routes.js:76 and the comment at storage.js:58 both treat the link as time-limited.

findings.title: Session tokens carry no expiry and the verifier checks none
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: session has no expiry
findings.evidence: decodeSession at server.js:13-33 splits the token, recomputes the HMAC over the payload, compares it in constant time and returns the parsed claims. No temporal claim is read: grep for exp, expires and ttl across server.js returns nothing, and the gate at server.js:62-74 branches only on whether claims is null. There is no server-side session record either, so nothing can revoke one. pulse-notify does check expiry at plugins/auth.js:28, so this is not a house convention.
findings.impact: A token captured once authenticates forever, and logout has nothing to invalidate. Combined with ORCH-09, which writes job payloads including tokens into the worker log, the window for a captured credential is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Include an exp claim in the payload, reject at or past it, and keep a revocation list keyed on a token id for the compromise case.

triage.reason: The middleware at server.js:62-74 is the only authentication layer and it performs no temporal check; no store is consulted.

A cookie Max-Age set by the issuer, which is outside this tree, would bound a compliant browser and not a holder of the token value, so it would not exculpate. No artifact for it arrived; recorded as UNKNOWN, and the severity is medium for it.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The worker logs the entire job payload on failure, including the caller-supplied callback token
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: worker logs full job payload incl. callbackToken
findings.evidence: worker/index.js:36 puts `payload: job.data` into the pino record, with the comment at :28-29 giving the reason ('Keep the whole payload on failures'). job.data for a render job is assembled at routes.js:20-27 and includes callbackToken, taken from body.callbackToken — a bearer secret the caller supplies so the completion callback can authenticate to their endpoint. No redaction is configured: pino's redact option is absent at worker/index.js:10 and at server.js:11. Retries make this likely rather than incidental: queue/index.js:13 sets attempts to 3.
findings.impact: Third-party callback credentials are written in clear text into the worker log on every failed job, so anyone with log access — an aggregator, an on-call engineer, a log-shipping vendor — holds them. WEB-22 names this precise pattern.
findings.recommendation: Configure pino's redact for callbackToken and any authorization-bearing field, or log an allowlist of correlation fields (jobId, tenantId, template) rather than the payload. Treat tokens already in the log as disclosed.

triage.reason: No redaction processor or serialiser filter is configured on either pino instance (worker/index.js:10, server.js:11).
callbackToken is by construction a credential — routes.js:24-26 sends it back on the completion callback so the caller can authenticate the call.
The handler is registered unconditionally in start() (worker/index.js:23-41), which is the shipped worker entry point at :61.

findings.title: The queue connection falls back to a hardcoded Redis password
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: hardcoded default Redis password
findings.evidence: queue/index.js:8 sets password: process.env.REDIS_PASSWORD || 'orchard-local-dev'. The same module is imported by both the API (src/api/routes.js:5) and the worker (src/worker/index.js:6), and package.json:8-9 runs both with NODE_ENV=production, so the production processes share this fallback. The correct pattern exists three files away: storage.js:27-29 throws when ORCHARD_ARTIFACT_SECRET is missing rather than substituting a literal.
findings.impact: Where REDIS_PASSWORD is unset, the queue is protected by a credential published in the repository. Redis holds every job payload — including the callbackToken of ORCH-09 and the tenant identifiers — and write access to the queue means arbitrary job injection into the worker, whose processors reach the filesystem (ORCH-05) and the network (ORCH-02).
findings.recommendation: Throw on a missing REDIS_PASSWORD as storage.js:28 does, and rotate the literal.

triage.reason: There is no environment gate on the fallback; it is evaluated at module load for every process, and package.json:8-9 shows both production entry points import it.
Secret-exposure finding; there is no attacker-controlled input to trace.
A deployment may set REDIS_PASSWORD, and no artifact for it arrived. That is UNKNOWN per FP-08 and does not affect the confirmed defect, which is the fail-open default plus the versioned literal.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: Headless Chromium renders attacker-influenced content with --no-sandbox
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: chromium --no-sandbox
findings.evidence: render.js:32-41 invokes chromium-headless with --no-sandbox as its first argument, opening a file:// page whose content the job payload shapes: the stylesheet href at render.js:57 comes from assetBaseUrl and manifest.css, both attacker-reachable through ORCH-01 and ORCH-02, and the document id is interpolated into an attribute at :58. The browser sandbox is the boundary that contains a renderer compromise; disabling it means a renderer bug is directly a worker-process compromise.
findings.impact: Removes the last isolation layer between untrusted web content and the worker process, which holds the Redis credential (ORCH-10), the artifact signing secret and write access to the export root.
findings.recommendation: Drop --no-sandbox and give the container the kernel capabilities the sandbox needs (or run with a seccomp profile that permits user namespaces) rather than turning the sandbox off. Running the renderer as an unprivileged user in a dedicated container is the usual fix.

triage.reason: INF-09's exculpation covers a documented system container whose function requires the privilege; a PDF renderer does not require a disabled sandbox, and no compensating seccomp or user-namespace configuration ships with the service — there is no Dockerfile or compose file in orchard-jobs at all.
The rendered page's stylesheet URL derives from job data (render.js:57), which ORCH-01 shows is caller-controlled.
This is not an absent defence in depth beside a working equivalent — no other isolation layer is declared anywhere in the service.

findings.title: No rate limit or quota anywhere in the service, in front of a queue that fans out expensive work
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: no rate limiting
findings.evidence: The middleware stack at server.js:38-77 is an error handler, a body parser, the webhook router, the session gate and the main router — no limiter, and package.json:13-22 lists no rate-limiting dependency. Each POST /v1/jobs enqueues a Chromium render with a 90-second timeout (render.js:40), retried up to three times (queue/index.js:13), against a worker pool of four (worker/index.js:15). POST /v1/exports permits rows up to 1,000,000 (schema.js:38). No per-tenant quota or budget exists.
findings.impact: Any authenticated tenant, or any partner reaching the webhook, can saturate the render and export pools and starve every other tenant, at a cost of one HTTP request per 90 seconds of worker CPU.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-identity limiter on the job-submitting routes, and a per-tenant concurrency budget on the queue, with cost proportional to the operation as WEB-18's exculpation describes.

triage.reason: No limiter exists at any layer in the repository; BullMQ's concurrency setting bounds the worker's parallelism, not any single tenant's share of it.
A gateway in front could throttle, but no deployment artifact ships with this service. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, and it is part of why the severity is low.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The top-level error handler returns the raw exception message
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs: error handler returns exception messages
findings.evidence: server.js:41-45 catches everything and sets ctx.body = { error: err.message } with ctx.status = err.status || 500. Deliberate 400s from schema.js:48-52 carry useful validation text, but an unexpected failure — an S3 error, a Redis connection error, a filesystem error from the processors — returns its internal message, including hostnames and paths, to the caller.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance detail about the internal topology, including bucket names, Redis endpoints and filesystem paths, returned to any caller who can provoke an unhandled error.
findings.recommendation: Return err.message only where err.status was set deliberately by application code, and a generic message with a correlation id otherwise.

triage.reason: No mapping layer stands between the throw and the response; server.js:43 assigns err.message directly.
The err.status check at :42 distinguishes status codes, not message provenance, so a 500-class internal message is returned by the same line.

findings.title: The production API task role inherits the AdministratorAccess managed policy
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: prod API task role = AdministratorAccess
findings.evidence: Three files join to make this. environments.ts:26-30 maps the ops tier to the literal 'AdministratorAccess'. environments.ts:68 sets prod.apiTier to 'ops', with the comment at :66-67 giving the reason ('The production API also exposes the maintenance commands the on-call runbooks use'). service-role.ts:43-46 resolves cfg.tierPolicies[cfg.apiTier] and calls role.addManagedPolicy(ManagedPolicy.fromAwsManagedPolicyName(policyName)) on the role constructed at :23-26, whose only other statement is a logs grant. api-stack.ts:33-36 builds that ServiceRole and :46 attaches it as the taskRole of the Fargate task definition that runs the internet-facing API (:76-93, an internetFacing ALB in front of it). Each file reads as reasonable in isolation; nothing in the tree flags that a tier name resolves to account-wide administrator for the one environment that matters.
findings.impact: Every application-level defect in the API container becomes full AWS account compromise in the production account: an SSRF that reaches the task metadata endpoint, or any code execution, yields credentials for a role that can read every bucket, every secret, create IAM principals and delete the account's resources. The three targeted grants immediately above it (api-stack.ts:39-41) are made redundant by it, which is the sign the intent was least privilege.
findings.recommendation: Delete the ops tier's AdministratorAccess mapping. Give the maintenance commands their own role assumed deliberately, with an explicit statement list, and leave the task role with the scoped grants api-stack.ts:39-41 already makes. Add a synth-time assertion that no task role carries an AWS-managed admin policy.

triage.reason: No condition, permissions boundary or SCP appears anywhere in the tree — service-role.ts:45 attaches the managed policy unconditionally, and cdk.json:7-15 contains only feature flags. INF-01's exculpation requires a guardrail in the same repository.
The privilege is not a bounded intended exposure: the role is attached to a task reachable from an internet-facing load balancer (api-stack.ts:78).
Both halves are in this repository — the tier mapping and the attachment — so nothing external needs to arrive for the join to be decidable.

findings.title: The production artifact bucket grants anonymous s3:GetObject over every object, and the same bucket holds rendered documents and tenant exports
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: prod artifacts bucket public-read over the whole bucket
findings.evidence: environments.ts:64 sets prod.assetsPublic = true, with the comment at :63 scoping the intent to 'the shared brand assets'. data-stack.ts:28-32 passes it through as publicRead. bucket.ts:33-40 then relaxes two of the four block-public-access flags (blockPublicPolicy and restrictPublicBuckets both false) and bucket.ts:55-64 adds a resource policy granting s3:GetObject to iam.AnyPrincipal on arnForObjects('*') — every key, not the brand-asset prefix. The scope mismatch is stated in the same repository: data-stack.ts:26-27 says 'One bucket holds everything the platform produces: the brand assets the CDN pulls, the rendered documents and the tenant data exports.' INF-02's exculpation asks exactly this question — verify what the pipeline writes there — and the answer is in the comment above the construct.
findings.impact: Every rendered document and every tenant data export in the production account is readable by any anonymous caller who knows or guesses the key. The construct's own docstring (bucket.ts:16-19, 'Public reads are opt-in') is accurate; the defect is that the opt-in is bucket-wide while the need is prefix-wide.
findings.recommendation: Scope the policy to the public prefix — arnForObjects('assets/*') — or, better, split the brand assets into their own bucket and serve them through a CloudFront origin access identity, leaving block-public-access fully on for the artifact bucket.

triage.reason: INF-02's public-assets-by-design exculpation is defeated by data-stack.ts:26-27, which states the same bucket receives rendered documents and tenant exports. The intended exposure is a prefix; what ships is the bucket.
No CDN origin identity is declared anywhere in the stacks — grep for CloudFront and OriginAccessIdentity across beacon-cdk returns nothing — so the alternative INF-02 names is absent.
The objects include tenant data exports per data-stack.ts:27.

findings.title: grantArtifacts is called without the prefix its own contract requires, granting the API role the whole bucket
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: grantArtifacts called without prefix → whole-bucket grant
findings.evidence: service-role.ts:48-51 documents the parameter: 'Pass the prefix the service writes under so the grant stays scoped to it.' The signature at :52-56 defaults prefix to '', and :60 then resolves to arnForObjects('*') with :67 setting the s3:prefix condition to '*'. api-stack.ts:39 is the function's only call site in the tree and passes two arguments, omitting the third. The contract is stated and unenforced — the default silently produces the unscoped grant the doc exists to prevent.
findings.impact: The API task role may Get, Put and Delete every object in the shared artifact bucket, including other services' rendered documents and every tenant's exports, and may list the whole bucket. In prod this is masked by BEACON-01, which is broader still; in dev and staging, where the tier is 'standard', this is the actual effective privilege.
findings.recommendation: Pass the prefix at api-stack.ts:39, and remove the default from the signature so omitting it is a compile error rather than a silent widening.

triage.reason: No condition narrows it: the ListBucket statement's StringLike condition at service-role.ts:67 evaluates to 's3:prefix': ['*'], which constrains nothing, and no SCP or boundary ships with the repository.
The default parameter is ordinary TypeScript; the call at api-stack.ts:39 supplies two of three arguments and the third takes its default of ''.
The intended bound is stated in the doc comment and is a prefix; the shipped grant is the bucket, so the exposure exceeds the intent rather than matching it.

findings.title: The Postgres instance is declared publiclyAccessible so a separate account can pull over the public endpoint
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: RDS publiclyAccessible true
findings.evidence: data-stack.ts:60 sets publiclyAccessible: true, with the comment at :58-59 giving the reason ('The analytics warehouse lives in a separate account and pulls nightly over the public endpoint'). It is a deliberate choice rather than an omitted default, and it applies to every environment because it is not derived from cfg. INF-04 lists 5432 among the ports that turn network exposure into a finding.
findings.impact: A production database is declared reachable from outside the VPC, with a generated master credential (data-stack.ts:38-40) as the only barrier, and no IAM authentication or client-certificate requirement declared. The cross-account pull it enables has no source restriction expressed anywhere in the repository.
findings.recommendation: Replace the public endpoint with VPC peering, PrivateLink or a scheduled export to S3 for the analytics account, and set publiclyAccessible: false. If the public endpoint must stay, restrict the security group to the warehouse's egress addresses and require TLS.

triage.reason: network-stack.ts:71-85 restricts the database security group to the service and bastion groups only, which is a real control — but it is the same control the comment says the nightly pull traverses, so either the pull does not work as described or a rule exists outside the repository. Neither reading exculpates the declaration.

data-stack.ts:48 places the instance in PRIVATE_ISOLATED subnets. AWS assigns a routable public address only where the subnet group has an internet gateway route, so this combination may make the flag inert in practice. Nothing in the repository settles whether the isolated subnets have such a route — network-stack.ts:32-36 declares them isolated, which suggests not. Per the triage contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, and it is reported as probable for that reason.
The exposure is intended but not bounded: no source CIDR, peering or endpoint restriction for the warehouse appears anywhere in the tree.

findings.title: The dev bastion accepts SSH from 0.0.0.0/0
findings.class: Management port open to the internet
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: dev adminCidrs 0.0.0.0/0 SSH
findings.evidence: environments.ts:36 sets dev.adminCidrs to ['0.0.0.0/0'] where staging (:49) and prod (:62) name specific ranges. network-stack.ts:52-58 loops over cfg.adminCidrs and adds an ingress rule on tcp/22 for each, so the dev bastion accepts SSH from anywhere. INF-04 places port 22 in the set that goes straight to a finding rather than to review. The blast radius is not confined to the bastion: network-stack.ts:81-85 grants the bastion group ingress to Postgres on 5432.
findings.impact: Unrestricted internet exposure of a management port in the dev account, and through the bastion's own database ingress rule, a path to the dev database. BEACON-07 makes this reachable by accident as well as by design, since an unset BEACON_ENV synthesises the dev config.
findings.recommendation: Give dev the same treatment as staging — a named range — or drop the bastion in favour of SSM Session Manager, which removes the ingress rule entirely.

triage.reason: INF-04's exculpation covers a public load balancer on 80/443, where being open is the point. This is tcp/22 on a jump host, and the field's own comment at environments.ts:8 says it is meant to hold 'ranges the operators reach the bastion from'.
A NACL or organization-level guardrail could narrow it, but INF-04 is explicit that an undeclared firewall must not be assumed, and none is declared in this repository. UNKNOWN, not HOLDS.
0.0.0.0/0 is by definition every principal on the internet.

findings.status_note: Downgraded from confirmed to probable because FP-08 is answered UNKNOWN. The triage contract caps a finding at probable when any invoked rule could not be established; the code fact in `evidence` is read directly from the tree and is not in doubt.

findings.title: The API task environment declares a CORS wildcard together with credentials
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: CORS * with credentials in task env
findings.evidence: api-stack.ts:53-61 sets CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN: '*' and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS: 'true' in the container environment, with the comment at :57-58 explaining that the origin cannot be pinned because tenants use their own subdomains. The pair is invalid by specification — browsers reject Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on a credentialed request — so an implementation that satisfies both settings has to reflect the request's Origin, which is the WEB-16 defect. This is the same mistake the sibling service edge-relay makes explicitly at nginx/relay.conf:39, which is what the configuration here describes in words.
findings.impact: If the image honours these settings by reflecting the origin, any page can read authenticated API responses in a victim's session across every tenant. If it honours them literally, credentialed cross-origin calls simply fail and the tenant subdomains break — so one of the two is true and both are defects.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the tenant-subdomain pattern the API should match against, anchored at both ends, and keep credentials only for origins that match it.

triage.reason: The consuming application is the beacon/api:1.12.0 image (api-stack.ts:50) and its source is not in this tree, so how it interprets the pair cannot be established here. Per the triage contract this caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed. The declaration itself is confirmed by reading api-stack.ts:59-60.
The credentials flag exists precisely because the responses are per-session, so they are not identical public data.
No layer overrides these values: the ALB listener at api-stack.ts:82-86 adds no header rules and no WAF is declared.

findings.title: pickEnv silently returns the dev configuration for any unrecognised environment name
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk: pickEnv silently falls back to dev
findings.evidence: environments.ts:82-84 returns environments[name ?? ''] ?? dev — no throw, no warning, no allowlist check. bin/beacon.ts:14 feeds it process.env.BEACON_ENV ?? app.node.tryGetContext('env'), and the comment at :12-13 says the pipeline exports BEACON_ENV per stage while a bare local synth is meant to fall back to sandbox settings. The map's keys are 'dev', 'staging' and 'prod' (:74), so any other spelling — an unset variable, or the common 'production' — resolves to dev, which is the environment carrying adminCidrs 0.0.0.0/0 (:36), assetsPublic true (:37) and ephemeral true (:38).
findings.impact: A typo or a dropped variable in the pipeline produces a synth that targets account 000000000001 with the world-open bastion rule and DESTROY removal policies, silently rather than failing. Because cfg.account also comes from the same object (bin/beacon.ts:16), the misdirection includes which account is deployed to, which limits the damage but hides the mistake.
findings.recommendation: Throw on an unknown or absent name, listing the valid keys. A deployment tool should refuse to guess which environment it is building.

triage.reason: pickEnv is the sole entry point used by the shipped app at bin/beacon.ts:14; there is no separate production path.

There is no equivalent check elsewhere — no validation of BEACON_ENV appears in bin/beacon.ts or cdk.json — so this is not an absent second layer beside a working first one. It ships as low because the account switch bounds the consequence.
The input is an operator-set environment variable in a deployment pipeline, not an attacker-controlled value; the finding is the fail-open default rather than an injection.
